title: Laser beams can chill atoms to a few millionths of a degree above absolute zero

cover.alt: The inside of a vacuum chamber glowing deep pink and red in laser light, seen through a curved window.

body: Lasers usually heat things, but tuned just right they can slow atoms almost to a standstill. The light is set slightly below the colour an atom absorbs, so only atoms moving towards a beam see it Doppler-shifted into tune; each photon they absorb nudges them backwards. With six beams crossing, atoms are slowed whichever way they move, and in a [magneto-optical trap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magneto-optical_trap) a weak magnetic field also pushes them back to the centre. Depending on the kind of atom, clouds caught this way can get as cold as a few microkelvin: millionths of a degree above absolute zero.

slides.alt: A view into a vacuum chamber lit pink and red by laser light. After about two seconds a small bright spot appears near the middle and grows into a glowing cloud.
slides.caption: A lab at the University of California, Santa Barbara: a bright cloud of trapped lithium atoms appears in the vacuum chamber and grows as more atoms are caught.

slides.prompt: Each absorbed photon kicks an atom backwards, but the atom then re-emits the light. Why doesn't that undo the slowing?
slides.answer: Re-emitted light flies off in random directions
slides.detail: The absorbed kicks all point against the atom's motion, but the emitted ones point every which way and average out, so over many cycles the atom slows down.

steps.label: Six laser beams cross inside a vacuum
Atoms moving into a beam absorb it and slow
A weak magnetic field steers them inwards
A cold, glowing cloud gathers in the middle

slides.heading: A Nobel Prize for cold atoms
slides.text: Steven Chu, Claude Cohen-Tannoudji and William Phillips shared the 1997 Nobel Prize in Physics for developing ways to cool and trap atoms with laser light. Laser cooling also helped make the first Bose–Einstein condensates in 1995.

slides.question: Why do laser-cooled atoms make atomic clocks more accurate?
options: Slow atoms blur the measurement less
slides.explanation: Fast atoms see the measuring light Doppler-shifted, which smears out the signal. Slowing them down removes most of that uncertainty.
